title: 3-Read Friday #58: AI Feedback, Homework, and Student Insights
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 58 mixes an AI-and-feedback piece with two pieces aimed more directly at students and their habits. Barton opens with Daisy Christodoulou's distinction between feedback that is accurate and feedback that is useful, noting the risk that AI-generated feedback could simply get better at being accurate without becoming any more useful -- the same trap he says teachers already fall into on a Sunday evening. He then recommends Jo Castelino's post on reframing homework for students, crediting her as the 'Queen of Homework' and highlighting the specific idea of changing how teachers talk about homework. His third pick is Jon Sellick's guide of insights for students to share directly with them, praising its mix of cognitive-science advice (spaced repetition) and life-skills advice (sleep, exercise).
points: Barton draws a direct parallel between AI-generated feedback and teachers' own Sunday-evening marking habits, suggesting AI risks automating an already low-value activity rather than fixing it.
His nickname for Castelino -- 'the Queen of Homework' -- signals a recurring-author relationship across issues, not a one-off discovery.

He singles out the reframing of how teachers talk about homework (not new homework tasks themselves) as the standout idea in Castelino's post, a subtle distinction about language and mindset over content.

His admission that he 'could use some of this advice myself' about Sellick's student-facing life-skills tips is a small but telling moment of the curator applying student-facing advice to his own habits.
quotes: Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.
Daisy draws the simple and yet powerful distinction between written feedback that is accurate and feedback that is useful.
Teachers often spend hours on a Sunday doing the former, and it seems AI might be falling into the same trap.
Reframing how we talk about homework to our students really stood out for me.
I love that it includes insights from cognitive science (spaced repetition), but also life skills such as sleeping well and exercising.
